title: The Fed and the Treasury Are in Denial
gist: Katharina Pistor argues the US can no longer count on the automatic global demand for its Treasury debt and dollars that defined the postwar era, and that policymakers cling to a discredited orthodoxy of self-correcting, efficient 'flat' markets rather than recognizing that markets are actively 'made'.

themes.theme: Erosion of US debt and dollar privilege

insights.claim: For most of the postwar era the United States enjoyed a privileged position as an issuer of both sovereign debt and dollars that always found takers, but it may no longer be able to rely on stable demand for either.
insights.speaker: KATHARINA PISTOR
insights.so_what: If auto-demand for Treasuries and dollars is weakening, term premia and funding costs could reprice structurally higher — a core macro risk for anyone long US duration or short volatility in rates.
insights.quote: the US may no longer be able to rely on stable demand for its debt or its currency, forcing policymakers to face the truth about how financial markets are made
insights.locator: For most of the postwar era

insights.claim: US policymakers are described as being 'in denial' about the fragility of demand for American debt and currency, forcing them to confront how financial markets are actually made rather than assuming they clear automatically.
insights.speaker: KATHARINA PISTOR
insights.so_what: Signals a regime where the Fed and Treasury may have to intervene more actively to sustain their own market — watch for backstops, buybacks, and liquidity facilities as recurring policy tools.
insights.locator: The Fed and the Treasury Are in Denial

insights.claim: The orthodoxy that markets are 'flat' and naturally pursue efficient outcomes still grips many economists and, more consequentially, policymakers, even as evidence mounts against it.
insights.speaker: KATHARINA PISTOR
insights.so_what: A shift away from efficient-markets dogma toward a 'markets are constructed' view reframes central-bank and regulatory action as market-making, not just refereeing — bullish for the durability of official-sector intervention.
insights.quote: the orthodoxy of “flat” markets in pursuit of efficient outcomes maintains its grip on the minds of many economists and, more problematically, policymakers
insights.locator: Today, we are at a similar juncture

insights.claim: Pistor likens today's dominant belief in efficient markets to the Catholic Church's centuries-long dogma that the world was flat and the sun revolved around it, implying a scientific-scale revolution is needed to dislodge it.
insights.speaker: KATHARINA PISTOR
insights.so_what: The framing implies entrenched intellectual resistance — policy adjustment to the new reality is likely to lag markets, leaving windows where official models misprice risk.
insights.quote: For centuries, the Catholic Church upheld the dogma that the world was flat and that the sun revolved around it, despite evidence to the contrary.
